# Multi-Client File and System Information Server made using code generated by ChatGPT - 5.6 Sol medium

A pure Java TCP client/server application supporting authenticated, concurrent file access and server-system queries. The server and every client run as separate JVM processes and may run on different computers.

## Requirements and build

Java 17 LTS or newer is recommended. Java 17 provides long-term support and all language/API features used here. Maven is the recommended build approach because it gives a conventional project layout, but there are no external dependencies.

### Maven

```text
mvn clean package
java -cp target/classes edu.cse593.fileserver.ServerMain 5050 shared 20 logs
java -cp target/classes edu.cse593.fileserver.ClientMain localhost 5050
```

### Plain javac (PowerShell)

```powershell
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force out | Out-Null
javac -d out (Get-ChildItem -Recurse src/main/java -Filter *.java).FullName
java -cp out edu.cse593.fileserver.ServerMain 5050 shared 20 logs
java -cp out edu.cse593.fileserver.ClientMain localhost 5050
```

Server arguments are `[port] [shared-directory] [worker-count] [log-directory]`; defaults are `5050 shared 20 logs`. The worker count must be at least 5. Client arguments are `[server-host] [port]`.

For two computers, run `ServerMain` on the server machine, permit inbound TCP traffic on the chosen port in its firewall, and run `ClientMain SERVER_IP 5050` on each client machine. Do not expose this classroom authentication scheme directly to the public internet: TCP content and passwords are not encrypted.

Predefined demonstration accounts:

| Username | Password |
|---|---|
| `admin` | `admin123` |
| `alice` | `alice123` |
| `bob` | `bob123` |

The connection closes after three failed login attempts.

## Project structure

```text
multi-client-file-server/
├── pom.xml                         Maven build configuration (Java 17)
├── README.md                       Build, run, design, and protocol documentation
├── .gitignore                      Generated/runtime file exclusions
└── src/main/java/edu/cse593/fileserver/
    ├── ServerMain.java             Server process entry point and argument parsing
    ├── ClientMain.java             Client process entry point and argument parsing
    ├── protocol/
    │   └── Protocol.java           Shared command/status/buffer constants
    ├── server/
    │   ├── FileServer.java         Socket accept loop, worker pool, and logging setup
    │   ├── ClientHandler.java      Authentication and command loop for one client
    │   ├── AuthService.java        Three predefined in-memory user accounts
    │   ├── FileService.java        Safe file operations and per-file read/write locks
    │   └── ServerState.java        Concurrent client counts and server uptime
    └── client/
        └── ConsoleClient.java      Text menu, protocol implementation, file transfers
```

At runtime the server creates `shared/` and `logs/` unless different paths are supplied. Only plain file names are accepted remotely; absolute paths, traversal, subdirectories, symbolic links, and internal temporary names are rejected. Uploads are written to a temporary file and then moved into place so clients do not see partial files.

## Application protocol

The connection is a stateful TCP stream implemented with buffered `DataInputStream` and `DataOutputStream`. Strings are Java modified UTF-8 frames (`writeUTF`/`readUTF`), counts use 32-bit signed integers, file sizes/timestamps use 64-bit signed longs, flags use booleans, and file content is exactly the announced number of raw bytes. Every request and response is flushed at its message boundary.

### Authentication

Client sends `UTF "AUTH"`, `UTF username`, `UTF password`. Server returns `UTF status`, `UTF message`, where status is `OK` or `ERROR`. On `ERROR`, the client may retry, up to three total attempts. No other command is accepted before authentication.

### Commands and responses

All commands begin with one UTF command token.

| Command request after token | Successful response after `UTF "OK"`, `UTF message` |
|---|---|
| `LIST` | `int count`, repeated (`UTF name`, `long size`, `long modifiedEpochMs`) |
| `DOWNLOAD`, `UTF name` | `long size`, then exactly `size` raw bytes |
| `DELETE`, `UTF name` | no payload |
| `INFO`, `UTF name` | `UTF name`, `long size`, `long modifiedEpochMs`, `boolean readable`, `boolean writable` |
| `TIME` | ISO-8601 UTC time in the response message |
| `UPTIME` | formatted JVM uptime in the response message |
| `MEMORY` | four longs: used, free, allocated/total, maximum JVM bytes |
| `CLIENTS` | two ints: connected and authenticated client counts |
| `THREADS` | three ints: thread-group estimate, live JVM threads, peak JVM threads |
| `EXIT` | no payload; server then closes the connection |

`UPLOAD` is intentionally two phase:

1. Client sends `UTF "UPLOAD"`, `UTF name`, `long size`.
2. Server validates metadata and returns `UTF "READY"`, `UTF message` (or `ERROR`).
3. Client sends exactly `size` raw bytes only after `READY`.
4. Server returns final `UTF "OK"`, `UTF message` after committing the file.

Except for the `READY` upload handshake, failures use `UTF "ERROR"`, `UTF human-readable-message` and have no payload.
